review.conclusion_reason: NO by June 14, 1900 does not follow from the upheld evidence. The officer eligibility condition is not an express sunset, and the Organic Act is a candidate replacement statute that does not name EO 116. OPEN is required: obtain evidence ending the covered officers' continuations, such as Presidential actions or documented replacement, and resolve the election clause's completion with an implementation source if relying on performance. The formal finding that no express ending was found is supportable only within the reviewed evidence. The original's accepted=true designation is also unverified: the held OCR identifies a 1902 compilation with publisher unrecorded, and the archive page could not be opened. Consequently T2's accepted-original prerequisite is unmet.
missed_evidence: The full officer-continuation sentence in jobs/tischendorf-originals/output/texts/EO_116.txt distinguishes eligibility before legislation from tenure at Presidential pleasure; this defeats p4's asserted express sunset.

https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Hawaiian_Organic_Act, section 80, adds 'but not beyond the end of the first session' to the transitional continuation. This is a more specific candidate endpoint than the quoted fragment, but neither establishes EO 116's ending nor supplies the session-end event evidence.
The first gap's GovInfo URL opens only printed page 141, not the full Act. It cannot alone verify sections 7, 8, 14, 80 and 104 on the other named pages.
review.stop_code_verdict: confirmed: WEB fits the first gap, which requires external Statutes at Large pages absent from the evidence slice. The supplied GovInfo URL contains only page 141; the remaining named pages still need verification.
review.suspected_defect: The central defect is treating an eligibility condition as an express termination in p4, then declaring NO despite the worker's own unresolved interpretation and performance gaps. The official_printing designation also overstates provenance that the worker explicitly left unchecked. Deliberateness cannot be determined.

verdicts.reason: Held EO_116.txt contains the May 13, 1899 date, McKinley signature, and quoted annexation-resolution authority. This confirms content, not official provenance.
Held text expressly directs that the specified September election shall not be held. It does not document subsequent compliance.
Held text expressly continues the covered elective officers at the President's pleasure.

The phrase 'whose terms of office shall expire before appropriate legislation shall have been enacted' defines which officers qualify. It does not expressly terminate their continuation when Congress legislates.

The cited Hawaii archive URL was inaccessible, but another cited source, https://hawaii-nation.org/organic.html, section 1 historical note, expressly confirms April 30 enactment and June 14, 1900 effect. The opened GovInfo page 141 also confirms the Act's date.
Opened Wikisource section 104 contains the quoted forty-five-day provision. It also excepts section 52, effective upon approval; the proposition requires that qualification.

Section 80 contains the quoted continuation language and a statutory tenure scheme, but does not name EO 116 or expressly terminate its Presidential-pleasure provision. Replacement of that provision is an inference, insufficient under the project rules.
Opened hawaii-nation.org section 7 expressly repeals the Republic's constitution. The awkward quoted wording is present. This establishes repeal of the constitution, not a named ending of EO 116.
Opened hawaii-nation.org section 14 explicitly schedules the general election in November 1900 and every second year thereafter.
Opened hawaii-nation.org section 8 expressly abolishes the enumerated principal offices. It does not establish disposition of every elective office covered by EO 116.
Both named held texts were opened and agree on the operative election and officer-continuation language.
The evidence slice and opened EO_3016J.txt show the match in a patent table, not a reference to EO 116. No named revocation appears in the supplied evidence; this finding is limited to that evidence.
